articles.title: ‘Few actors possessed his intensity’: PM Modi mourns Nana Patekar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday condoled veteran actor Nana Patekar, remembering his “immense” contribution to Hindi and Marathi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday condoled veteran actor Nana Patekar, remembering his “immense” contribution to Hindi and Marathi cinema and praising his versatility and creativity.In a post on X, PM Modi wrote: “Few actors possessed the intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence that Shri Nana Patekar Ji had. He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations. He was also admired for his frank and forthright views, never hesitating to express what he believed in.”He added: “Shri Nana Patekar’s contribution to Hindi and Marathi cinema was immense. His passing leaves a deep void. My condolences to his family, friends and countless admirers. Om Shanti.”While speaking at an event in Delhi, PM Modi remembered veteran actor.“This morning we got the news that the renowned actor Nana Patekar is no longer with us. He was an exceptional artist who won the hearts of audiences through a variety of roles,” PM Modi said.The Prime Minister said Patekar’s life was dedicated to the “honour and glory of the Tricolour” and used references to some of the actor’s well-known films to describe his career.“Nana Patekar’s life was dedicated to the honour and glory of the Tricolour. He refused to be bound by constraints; like a ‘Parinda’, he soared through the vast skies of cinema,” PM Modi said.He said Patekar used his films to raise questions about social issues and challenge the prevailing order.“Through his films, he launched scathing attacks on the prevailing societal order. He was a true Krantiveer who fought against social evils,” PM Modi said.PM also recalled Patekar’s distinctive screen presence, saying, “His silence was as impactful as his speech was powerful.”The Prime Minister said Patekar consistently spoke against anti-national elements and paid tribute to the actor while offering condolences to his family and admirers.“I pay tribute to Nana Patekar and offer my condolences to his family and admirers,” PM Modi said.Meanwhile, Union home minister Amit Shah also mourned Patekar, sharing a picture with the veteran actor and calling his passing an “irreparable loss” to the world of art.In a post, Shah wrote: “Over five decades, with his natural acting and powerful dialogue delivery, he left an indelible mark on the hearts of audiences. Whether it was serious social issues or humor-satire, he brought to life every character he portrayed. Through the 'Naam Foundation,' serving drought-stricken farmer families, or going to the border to boost the morale of soldiers, even after reaching the pinnacle of fame, he remained connected to his roots.”He added: “Whenever I met him, his simplicity and straightforwardness always left a deep impression. May God grant strength to the grieving family and fans to bear this sorrow, and may the departed soul find a place at His divine feet.”Defence minister Rajnath Singh also paid tribute to Patekar, writing: “Nana Patekar was not merely an actor; he was an institution in himself. His remarkable contribution to Indian cinema will continue to inspire generations.”Patekar suffered a cardiac arrest at his home in Goa and was found unconscious. He was rushed to a hospital, where doctors declared him dead.Known for films including Prahaar, Parinda, Krantiveer, Tirangaa and Welcome, Patekar was one of the most recognised actors in Hindi and Marathi cinema.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: After more than six generations of family ownership, a Massachusetts nonprofit raised over $4.9 million to buy 5.23-acre Holly Hill Farm and permanently protect the centuries-old piece of farmland
articles.summary: For generations, Holly Hill Farm belonged to the same family.
articles.body: For generations, Holly Hill Farm belonged to the same family. Now, after more than six generations of White family ownership, the 5.23-acre Massachusetts property has been secured for the future as a working farm, thanks to a fundraising effort by Friends of Holly Hill Farm (FHHF), according to a report by Cohasset Anchor. The nonprofit raised more than $4.9 million to buy the land and invest in its buildings and infrastructure, including $1 million in community preservation funds from the Town of Cohasset. This September 2026 purchase means the farm will remain a working farm and community resource permanently.FHHF will own and operate the farm, and a Conservation Restriction (CR) has also been placed on the part of the land that was not previously protected. The restriction, jointly held by Wildlands Trust and the Town of Cohasset, will permanently prevent future development on the land.“This is a once-in-a-generation accomplishment for the community, and a huge win for the environment and this beautiful farm. We are incredibly grateful to the White family and the community of Keep Our Farm a Farm supporters who made it possible to protect this precious land. However, our farm is more than the land, and we’re asking the community to join us to help ensure we can grow, teach, and be here for the community for generations to come,” Meredith Laban, Executive Director of Friends of Holly Hill Farm, said in a statement.Jean White, the co-founder of the farm, said this moment is a fulfilment of her husband Frank’s wishes. “Our family is enormously grateful for the efforts expended by all those in the community who worked on this initiative and the many extraordinary friends who helped make this happen. This teaching farm is a community resource for all ages, and will be preserved in perpetuity.”Though the land is protected, the nonprofit will continue to raise funds for its next phase, including making improvements to the historic 1785 barn, which houses the year-round farm stand. Better traffic flow and parking, as well as a heated, year-round indoor classroom with a working kitchen for teaching and preparing food for pantries, plus restrooms, are also part of the upcoming phase.Mark DeGiacomo, Board Chairperson of FHHM, remembered the efforts of its pioneers. “We want to honour our nonprofit’s co-founders, Jean and Frank White, and their family for their generosity, vision, and unwavering commitment to sustainable farming, education, community, and the land. Their passion and dedication laid the groundwork for Friends of Holly Hill Farm, shaped its mission, impacted the lives of countless people, and helped make the farm the community treasure it is to so many. We remain committed to keeping our farm a farm, to growing its future, and working with the community to ensure we can be here for many years to come.”Beyond the vegetable rowsHolly Hill is a certified organic farm growing vegetables, herbs, seedlings and flowers. The harvest travels further than the farm stand. Through its Farm to Food Pantry programme, food and flowers go to nine local food pantries. The stand supplies participating families through the Holly Hill Farm SHARES programme and accepts SNAP. There are also educational programmes. More than 20,000 students from over 14 communities take part in programmes on the farm, in classrooms and in school gardens each year, and partnerships reach more than 40 schools between the South Shore and Boston. The summer programmes have been named Best of the South Shore four years running.Adults also get workshops and guided walks led by the farm’s educators and outside experts. Tiered pricing and scholarships are offered so cost does not keep anyone out. It is a community deeply passionate about the land and its natural resources.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'No excuse for victim blaming': Mamdani under fire from Democrats and pro-Palestinian left over Oct 7 message
articles.summary: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s statement marking the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel has drawn criticism from both sides of
articles.body: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s statement marking the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel has drawn criticism from both sides of the US political divide. Democrats and Jewish groups accusing him of shifting attention from the victims of the attack to Israel’s war in Gaza, while some on the pro-Palestinian left say he did not go far enough.Mamdani’s statement began by calling October 7, 2023, a “profoundly painful” day and condemning Hamas’ “horrific war crimes”, including the killing of about 1,200 people in Israel and the taking of more than 250 hostages.“We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he said.But Mamdani then turned to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, calling it a “devastating, ongoing genocide” and citing more than 74,000 deaths recorded by the Hamas-controlled Gaza health ministry.“Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani said.He added that three years later, “occupation and apartheid continue”, while accusing the US federal government of complicity through arms shipments.The statement drew fierce criticism from several Democratic lawmakers, who said Mamdani had made the anniversary about Israel rather than Hamas and the people killed and abducted on October 7.Florida representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz accused Mamdani of “desecrating the memory of murdered, innocent Jews”, while New Jersey representative Josh Gottheimer said the mayor was “blaming the victims”. Jersey City mayor Steven Fulop called the statement “inappropriate and unnecessarily inflammatory”.New York representative Dan Goldman called the message “egregious and insulting”. Goldman told Politico that October 7 should be reserved for remembering what he described as a horrific terror attack, rather than using the occasion to focus on the broader conflict.“Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming,” Goldman said.Brad Lander, the Mamdani-backed Democrat who defeated Goldman in this year’s primary, took a more nuanced position. He condemned Hamas but argued against forcing people to choose between mourning the victims of October 7 and acknowledging Palestinian suffering.“We can mourn for those lost on October 7th and still acknowledge the enormous imbalance of power between Israel and the Palestinians,” Lander wrote.Mamdani also faced criticism from Jewish organisations. Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said the mayor’s statement did not mention Jews and accused him of using a day meant for mourning the victims of the attack to repeat his anti-Zionist arguments.US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called the statement an “outrageous & disgusting rant”, while Ofir Akunis, Israel’s consul general in New York, called it a “disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered”.But the backlash did not come only from critics of Mamdani’s position on Israel.Pro-Palestinian left's critique of Mamdani Some on the pro-Palestinian left also attacked the mayor, arguing that his stance did not go far enough. About 200 anti-Israel protesters gathered outside City Hall on Wednesday evening, with some accusing Mamdani of betraying the Palestinian cause.Several protesters told Politico they had voted for Mamdani but would not support him for re-election because they were unhappy that he had not fired NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch, whom they described as a Zionist, or stopped some New York synagogues from hosting events promoting land sales in the occupied West Bank.The protesters’ criticism reflected a broader frustration among some activists that Mamdani, despite his longstanding opposition to Israel’s policies, had not gone far enough in confronting Israel or supporting the Palestinian cause.At the same time, senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who is a close adviser to Mamdani, defended the mayor’s basic framing of the conflict. Sanders said Israel had the right to defend itself and target Hamas after the October 7 attack, but accused Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government of waging “a genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza”.Mamdani’s statement had drawn more than 11 million views on X by Wednesday eveningThe controversy reflects the difficult political position Mamdani has occupied throughout his rise to power. His strong criticism of Israel helped energise young and progressive voters during his mayoral campaign, while also making him a frequent target of Jewish groups, Israeli officials and more moderate Democrats.Mamdani has consistently rejected accusations of antisemitism, arguing that criticism of Israel and its government is distinct from hostility towards Jewish people.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is ‘enemy property’ and how is it identified? Allahabad high court explains
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Can the government stop construction on a property merely by claiming that it is \"enemy property\" or \"evacuee property\"?
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Can the government stop construction on a property merely by claiming that it is "enemy property" or "evacuee property"? The Allahabad high court recently made some observations while hearing a dispute over a 90-square-metre plot in Muzaffarnagar. The court found that the authorities had not produced records showing that the property was formally recorded as either enemy or evacuee property and restrained them from interfering with the owners' possession and construction covered by a sanctioned map.What was the dispute over the property?According to the court order, the property was part of a plot in Civil Lines South, Muzaffarnagar. The petitioners claimed ownership through a chain of transactions going back to 1946.The property was initially owned by Nawab Mohammad Sadakkat Ali Khan. It was later transferred through an exchange deed, gift deed and family settlement. A civil court decree in 1956 declared Surendra Prakash the exclusive owner of the relevant property. After his death, the property devolved on the first two petitioners, who sold 90 square metres to the other petitioners through a registered sale deed in 2018.The petitioners obtained a sanctioned construction map in August 2018 and started developing a commercial complex.Why did the authorities stop the construction?Several complaints were made alleging that the land was enemy property. An inquiry by the District Magistrate rejected one such complaint in November 2018. Another complaint was rejected by the Muzaffarnagar Development Authority in January 2019.However, in January 2023, state officials stopped the construction. The petitioners alleged that officials later partly demolished the construction and marked the property as "Nishkrant Sampatti", or evacuee property.The State argued that since the original owner had become a Pakistani resident after Partition, the property could be treated as enemy property under the Enemy Property Act, 1968 or as evacuee property under the earlier 1950 law.But the counsel appearing for the Custodian of Enemy Property told the court that the property was not enemy property.What is enemy property?The Enemy Property Act, 1968 covers property belonging to, held by or managed on behalf of an "enemy", "enemy subject" or "enemy firm".The high court noted that an order passed by the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property on August 2, 2019 had already recorded that the relevant land was not enemy property. It also noted that the Custodian's own counter affidavit said the property had not been recorded as enemy property in official records."Thus, once the order dated 02.08.2019 had been passed by the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property, the reliance placed by the State-respondents on the communication dated 19.01.2019 to treat the property in question as enemy property, is misplaced and has no relevance at all," the court noted.The court therefore rejected the State's reliance on the earlier communication to justify treating the property as enemy property.What about the claim that it was evacuee property?The State also claimed that the disputed land had been evacuee property since 1947.The high court, however, found that the State had not produced documents showing that the property had ever been formally recorded as evacuee property. A 2021 letter referred to an earlier 2020 communication, but that communication itself was not placed before the court.The court also noted that the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 and the rules framed under it set out a procedure for identifying and recording evacuee properties, including the publication of lists."Since the respondents State has not brought on record any such document, which would refer the property in question either registered as an evacuee property or any such proceedings are still pending for its registration etc., mere allegation would not suffice and the action of the State respondents for stopping the constructions work on the land in question, where the map has been sanctioned, cannot be justified," the bench observed.This became a key reason for the court to reject the State's stand.Can authorities stop construction merely by making such a claim?A bench of Justice Vivek Saran and Justice Prakash Padia of the Allahabad high court said that a mere allegation was not enough.The court also noted that the development authority's sanctioned map remained valid and that the authority itself was not proceeding against the petitioners.The court also relied on the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the Custodian of Enemy Property, which the bench treated as an admission. The affidavit stated: "as per official records the said property in dispute has not yet been recorded as Enemy Property in the records of the respondent herein."The court found that the material placed before it did not establish that the property was enemy or evacuee property.The high court restrained the respondents from interfering with the petitioners' peaceful possession and occupation of the property.The protection was limited to the 90-square-metre portion for which construction had been sanctioned. The court allowed the petition and imposed no costs. Its operative direction is the restraint on interference, and the order does not separately direct removal of the signage. In effect, the order protects the petitioners on the sanctioned portion and does not extend to any construction beyond the approved map.

articles.title: Hygiene poverty at tipping point, charity warns
articles.summary: The BBC hears people "you would not expect" can no longer afford items to be clean and healthy.
articles.body:
People are increasingly unable to afford items they need to feel clean and healthy, a charity has warned.

Rosemary Ashworth, deputy chief executive of The Hygiene Bank, told BBC Radio Surrey the "face" of hygiene poverty had changed and it was affecting people who previously felt financially secure.

"We're at a bit of a tipping point so now feels like the time to do something about it," she said.

Janice Sedgwick, a volunteer at the charity's Guildford branch, said needed items were things like "toothbrushes, toothpaste, shower gel, shampoo, sanitary pads and laundry detergent".

But she said people were also struggling to get products to keep their houses clean.

A recent survey of 3,042 UK adults by The Hygiene Bank and In Kind Direct suggested one in five (18%) had experienced hygiene poverty in the last six months, or someone in their household had.

The charities said two in five (41%) of those affected said they had experienced it for the first time this year.

The Hygiene Bank said the phenomenon "can create a vicious cycle, affecting health, confidence, education, work and social participation".

Ashworth said "It's not people who [you] might necessarily expect experiencing it," she said. "It's working families. People who previously felt financially secure...

"It feels like a problem that is worsening."

Tom May, from Guildford-based mental health charity Oakleaf, said a common issue was women needed hygiene products on a "certain basis", though stores were "pretty much empty by the end of the week".

The Hygiene Bank is urging people to donate essential products or money for National Hygiene Week, which ends on 11 October.

articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
articles.summary: Many Palestinians are still living in cramped tent cities, with the US plan to end the war largely stalled.
articles.body:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.

"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.

He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.

"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.

Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.

She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.

On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.

But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.

Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.

"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.

In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.

The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.

Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.

"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."

Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.

The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.

On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.

His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.

The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.

Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.

Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.

Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.

The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.

In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.

In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.

Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.

"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.

Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.

Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.

"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.

"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."

There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.

The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.

Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.

Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.

Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.

Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).

But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.

"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."

articles.title: New Type 01 electric car 'make or break' for Jaguar
articles.summary: Prof David Bailey says there is a lot riding on the Type 01 in terms of jobs and investment.
articles.body:
Jaguar's new electric car represents "make or break" for the brand, an industry expert has said.

Parent company JLR has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and has faced mixed reactions over the design of the Type 01, which was unveiled this week.

Last month, it emerged Jaguar Land Rover, which has manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood on Merseyside, is to cut 4,000 jobs as it struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs and the transition to electric.

David Bailey, professor of business economics at the University of Birmingham, said it was a "perfect storm" for the firm, which has struggled since a cyber attack last year.

"I think it's make or break for Jaguar as a brand," he said of the Type 01 launch.

"Clearly it was failing to compete in the premium market, they've had to completely reinvent it, take it luxury and electric and that is a big gamble."

Bailey said the market for luxury electric cars was in its infancy, but that "Jaguar is right at the forefront of that".

He added: "It's going to have to create a whole new market where one didn't exist before, so it's a big, big gamble for the company."

Last month, Bentley unveiled its first fully electric car, the Torcal , after investing £350m to upgrade its factory in Crewe.

At the time, the government hailed the news, adding that it followed multimillion-pound investments by McLaren and Nissan in the UK car industry.

The minimum cost of Jaguar's Type 01 is £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US.

The new model's electric motors produce about 1,000 horsepower, allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds.

JLR, which has its global headquarters at Whitley in Coventry, says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.

The car was designed and built in the West Midlands and transferred to Manhattan for the launch.

The vehicles will be assembled at Lode Lane in Solihull, while their battery packs are being made at the Wolverhampton plant.

The cyber-attack caused JLR, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Bailey said the firm was facing tariffs from the US and "huge pressure to go electric".

"So the company itself is struggling, [has] announced 4,000 redundancies, so there's a lot riding on this car in terms of jobs and investment."

Jaguar's pivot to become an all-electric brand is seen by many in the industry as a high-risk decision.

Speaking last month, Kevin Moreley, a former managing director of the Rover Group, said the Type 01 would be a pivotal moment for the firm.

He said the 4,000 job losses would not be the end of the cuts if the car "doesn't sell the numbers they hope".

While JLR does not break down its accounts by brand, Jaguar is widely believed to be the worst performer in the group.

West Midlands mayor Richard Parker, meanwhile, has suggested the race to electric could be happening too quickly for consumers and that it could lead to production shifting elsewhere.

He has has called for the government's electric vehicle targets to be slashed to protect the sector.

The Type 01's looks have had a mixed response, but West Midlands members of the Jaguar Enthusiasts Club, which has 11,800 members worldwide, have welcomed the new model.

One of them, Tim Brookes, from Kingswinford, said he thought it would be "fantastic".

"I like that it's typically Jaguar as it's low, long, wide. It looks beautifully made... Although it looks like it's got the Jaguar heritage, everything about it looks fresh and new."

Ian Martin stated: "It's quite a bold statement and I think you have to be bold to compete and take Jaguar into a new market."

Peter Bennett, from Walsall, also a member of the group, said the level of technology in the new car and those that follow it "is way in advance of anything that we've seen".

"But the Chinese are bringing out cars for a lot less money with similar technology, so it's going to be tough, but I just hope that it works out for them."

Trainee car mechanics at City of Wolverhampton College also liked what they saw with the new car.

Student Muhammad Ali Adnan said: "I think I could see this in a James Bond movie in the future.

"[It] is very different from the old ones they made, so I think this is a risk and I think it has a potential to go positive."

articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg's nonprofit Biohub aims to prevent and cure diseases through virtual cells; gets millions from Google and US government; AI datasets may allow researchers to 'ask, predict, and answer biological questions digitally'
articles.summary: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan's nonprofit Biohub has brought Google, Meta and the US government into its plan to build a \"virtual cell\".
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan's nonprofit Biohub has brought Google, Meta and the US government into its plan to build a "virtual cell". A virtual cell is an AI model of human biology that can predict how cells behave, fall sick and respond to treatment. With the new commitments, total funding for the effort has reached $1.8 billion. Biohub says this is the largest coordinated investment in AI-ready biological data so far.Google DeepMind, Meta and Alphabet-owned drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs are jointly putting in $300 million. The US Department of Energy (DOE) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have also signed on. The money will build open datasets that could let researchers "ask, predict, and answer biological questions digitally". In practice, scientists could test ideas on a computer before taking them to a lab bench.How the $1.8 billion Biohub funding is splitDOE will invest more than $500 million over five years through its Genesis Mission. That money covers lab measurement, modelling and computation. It will use exascale supercomputers, cryo-electron microscopy and autonomous labs across the US National Laboratory system.NIH is not writing a fresh cheque. Under its Bio Genesis Mission, the agency will pool datasets and repositories built with over $500 million in earlier federal funding. Biohub will then standardise them for AI training. NIH's own announcement calls the target "SI-ready" data, short for super intelligence. Biohub uses the term AI-ready.Biohub anchored the Virtual Biology Initiative with $500 million in April 2026. Of that, $400 million goes into new measurement technology. This includes cryo-electron tomography, which resolves near-atomic detail inside a cell, and microscopy that can image millions to billions of cells in living tissue. The other $100 million funds research outside Biohub. Nvidia is offering computing infrastructure and software. The Broad Institute, Allen Institute, Wellcome Sanger Institute and the Human Cell Atlas are among the scientific partners.Virtual cell models need billions of cells to learn fromToday's cell datasets run to hundreds of millions of cells, Biohub's head of science Alex Rives told Reuters. He said an accurate predictive model will need billions and eventually trillions. The new measurements will come from techniques such as spatial transcriptomics, which maps molecular activity inside intact tissue. They will also come from screens that record how cells react when their environment changes.The timeline is tight. Rives said work like this would normally take decades. The partners want to finish it in five years, and the first dataset should be ready in about a year."An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally," Rives said in a statement. He called the virtual cell "one of the most important challenges for the next era of science."Google and Meta get early access before the data goes publicBiohub calls the project open science, but corporate funders get a head start. Companies that fund the project can work on the datasets for a fixed period before anyone else, Rives told Reuters. After that, the data becomes publicly available. The government-funded work will carry no such restriction. Biohub plans to approach pharmaceutical companies and philanthropies next.Other AI companies are moving into biology as well. Anthropic has set up its own wet lab. The OpenAI Foundation has launched a grant programme worth more than $125 million for biological and medical datasets.For Zuckerberg and Chan, the virtual cell has been a long-running goal. Biohub launched in 2016 with $600 million from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative's $3 billion pledge. That pledge aimed to cure or manage all diseases within their children's lifetime. One of Biohub's first projects was a cell atlas. In 2023, it started building a cluster of over 1,000 Nvidia H100 GPUs to model cells. Nearly a decade later, the goal remains the same, and Google, Meta and two US government agencies are now helping pay for the data it needs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Sutton-on-the-Forest solar farm recommended for approval by council
articles.summary: Officers say the benefits of producing renewable energy outweigh any harm the plans may create.
articles.body:
Plans for a solar farm on agricultural land in North Yorkshire have been recommended for approval despite concerns from residents about the loss of productive farmland.

Ampyr Solar Europe is seeking permission to build and operate a 49.9MW solar farm on 235 acres (75 ha) land at Brownmoor Lane, south-west of Sutton-on-the-Forest.

The development would include ground-mounted solar panels up to three metres high (10ft), a 10MW battery energy storage system, a new substation, access tracks, fencing and CCTV.

North Yorkshire Council's strategic planning committee are due to consider the application on 13 October, with planning officers recommending permission is granted.

Nine objections have been received, with concerns including the loss of agricultural land, the impact on a tenant farming business and whether solar panels should instead be installed on brownfield sites and buildings.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , Huby Parish Council said in its objection that solar farms "should not be built on arable land" only on "brownfield sites and existing commercial and domestic roofs".

Concerns were also been raised about the effect on the countryside and biodiversity, construction traffic and whether the scheme prioritised commercial interests over food production and the landscape.

However, planning officers concluded the agricultural impact did not justify refusing permission.

They also highlighted that the development would be temporary and reversible.

Permission has been sought for a 50-year operational period, after which the infrastructure would be removed and the land returned to agricultural use.

Although arable production would cease during that period, sheep grazing could continue beneath and between the solar panels.

The council report stated that the development's location was also influenced by the need to be close to a suitable electricity grid connection.

Officers concluded the public benefits of producing renewable energy outweighed the residual harm caused by the development.

articles.title: 'Emmeline Pankhurst is a gift of a role' says Beverley Knight
articles.summary: The Wolverhampton-born singer stars as suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst in Sylvia the musical.
articles.body:
Singer Beverley Knight said she hoped audiences watching her latest musical would leave feeling "empowered" and with the belief that their voices can make a difference.

Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and the family rift caused by the fight for women's voting rights.

The Wolverhampton artist, who plays Sylvia's mother and suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst at the Birmingham Hippodrome said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role".

"It's an absolutely killer story, and the best thing is it's true," she said.

"I want everyone bouncing out of there because it's a joyful musical, even though there's some absolutely heartbreaking moments in it."

The soul singer, known for hits including Shoulda Woulda Coulda and Get Up, told BBC Radio WM the musical was telling a "huge part of British history" from 1903, all the way to 1928.

"So most people know who Emmeline Pankhurst was, leader of the suffragettes, she was determined to get women the vote," she explained.

"But she came up against her middle daughter Sylvia, who not only wanted to get wealthy property owning women the vote, which was the case with men in the country, [you] had to be rich and male to vote, she wanted everybody to be able to vote.

"But Emmeline was focused on just the women and that put her on a collision course with her daughter and both of them were on a collision course with the government."

Knight added the show, which also features Naomi Katiyo as Sylvia Pankhurst, was "musically up my street" and was being called a "hip-hop musical" because it included elements of R&B, funk, soul, garage, gospel and house.

"The engine of the show is the music," she said. The whole thing is either spoken or rapped or sung. Of course, I'm doing mostly singing because I ain't rapping anything."

The former Highfields School pupil explained the story also went beyond the Pankhurst family, with some people who attended the show likely to have relatives who were involved in the suffragette movement.

"It's not just the story of the Pankhursts, there are going to be loads of people who will come to this show who will be like... my grandma or my great-grandma, she was involved in the suffragette movement.

"I want everybody to leave like, let's go, oh my god, that feeling of I can effect change, I can use my voice and effect change. I feel empowered."
